key_points: The shared vision is a world in which every human can freely share in all knowledge, and the movement has much more to do after 15 years.
Diversity and inclusivity are core values; the conference set an example with more than 100 scholarships (25% for women) and a code of conduct.
India has about one Wikimedia volunteer per million people, so these volunteers deserve investment as the future of the movement.
Indian communities achieved a lot: over 2,200 Punjabi articles at the conference edit-a-thon, a hackathon at IIT Roorkee, Wikipedia Asian Month, and Odia Wikipedia's 14th birthday.
Tulu Wikipedia went live that weekend after work since 2014.

The Wikimedia Foundation keeps the projects running and supports communities with grants, training, legal defence, communications and fundraising, funded by about 2.5 million donors giving around $15 on average.
The Foundation is investing in community capacity development, Indic script support and search, the content translation tool (100,000 articles translated) and OCR for Indic languages on Wikisource.
The New Readers initiative targets countries such as India where internet access is growing fast but awareness of Wikimedia is low; about half a billion people visit the projects each month.
Community health is a priority: the projects should feel as welcoming as in-person events, so that 'anyone can edit' is true.
The Foundation will invest in leadership development and encourages Indian Wikimedians to join movement governance; nobody from the region is on the Board of Trustees.
A movement-wide strategy process will be proposed by November and start in early 2017, and everyone is invited to take part.
The Foundation follows the lead of communities on smaller and emerging languages rather than having a fixed strategy for them.
Governments are big producers of knowledge, and local affiliates can partner with them and with cultural institutions without waiting for the strategy.
Strategy will likely need to be nuanced by region rather than one plan for the whole world, so voices from India need to be heard.
The Foundation acknowledges it communicates its resources poorly and is centralizing them, running a community wishlist, and writing technical collaboration guidelines.
The Foundation should go where users already are, including off-wiki channels like Facebook, WhatsApp and Telegram, and understand why people don't contribute.
Chapters should plan around what they are uniquely good at locally and what nobody else is doing.
